newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada vows to set own salmon fishing quotas.
newsitem.headline: Canada vows to set own salmon fishing quotas.

text.p: Canada, seeking to resolve its salmon fishing dispute with the United States, will set its own fishing quotas with a particular emphasis on conservation, Fisheries Minister David Anderson said on Thursday.

"Canada will not allow the salmon resource to suffer the consequences (of failed talks). We will establish our own fishing arrangements so that conservation is paramount," Anderson said in Ottawa, noting that he would make details of the quotas known shortly.

As tension escalated over the issue, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday that since the United States rejected Canada's latest offer on Monday, the best way to deal with the dispute over the West Coast salmon fishery is through a binding dispute settlement for a long-term solution.

"This outcome is very disappointing. Canada was ready to make a deal that would create a more stable regime and uphold the principles of the Pacific Salmon treaty," Axworthy said in a statement. "After months of negotiations, the U.S. offer has not changed signficantly. We need a new approach."

Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for the past few months on how to divide the Pacfic salmon catch. Both sides had hoped to reach an agreement before the fast-approaching salmon season started.
Talks initially broke down in May after Canada accused the United States of bargaining in bad faith.
The governments of Canada and the province of British Columbia threatened reprisals to pressure the United States into establishing fishing quotas.

Canada announced last month that it would begin enforcing requirements that U.S. boats fishing in Canadian waters must report to Canadian authorities. Under that policy, the Canadian Coast Guard temporarily seized four U.S. fishing boats.
However, the United States has blamed Canada for the breakdown in talks, saying Ottawa has been unwilling to make efforts to conserve salmon stocks off the West Coast.
